chunks: Why a crushed clock window hurts. The question: Why is crushing the clock window bad? How can this impact other circuits that may be connected to the clock?
The "clock window" is the time you get in each clock cycle to send data through the logic and have it caught safely at the other end.
If you shrink that window, by running faster or by letting the clock wobble, the data may not arrive in time. Then the chip makes errors.
Picture a relay race where each runner has one second to carry the baton and hand it over. The hand-over only works if the next runner is ready.
If the runner takes longer, or the starting signal comes at a slightly different time each lap, then some hand-overs fail.
The track doesn't care about the average lap; it only cares about the worst one.
One 1 nanoseconds cycle drawn to scale.
Launch clock-to-Q (120 picoseconds), logic (600 picoseconds), setup (60 picoseconds), skew (40 picoseconds) and jitter (50 picoseconds) add to 870 picoseconds, leaving 130 picoseconds of slack.
Crushing the window means eating that green slack.
Setup time: how long data must be steady before the clock edge arrives. Jitter: cycle-to-cycle variation in the clock edge timing.
Skew: a difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops. Metastability: a flip-flop output hovering between 0 and 1 because the data changed too close to the clock edge.
Flip-flop (flop): a tiny memory cell that grabs its input at each clock edge and holds it until the next.
A 1 gigahertz clock gives a 1 nanoseconds window. The launching flop takes 0. 2 nanoseconds to put out new data, the logic 0. 5 nanoseconds, setup 0.
1 nanoseconds, and skew plus jitter 0. 1 nanoseconds. That totals 0. 9 nanoseconds, so the margin is 0. 1 nanoseconds. Now let the PLL add another 0. 15 nanoseconds of jitter.
The total becomes 1. 05 nanoseconds, which is more than the window, so the margin is -0. 05 nanoseconds and the data is captured wrong. That is the whole idea.
"I take the clock window as the time you have each cycle for launch, logic, setup, skew and jitter.

If you crush it, with a faster clock, jitter, duty-cycle error or PLL overshoot, you get setup and hold violations and metastability in synchronous logic, minimum-pulse-width failures in flops and memories, SNR loss in ADCs through aperture jitter, and eye closure and bit errors in serial links and DDR.
Circuits see the worst cycle, not the average, so the failures are intermittent. You fix it with margin, cleaner clocks and holding logic in reset until lock."
